transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-09
Time: 08:00 PT / 16:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Rios (Redwood SE), Daniel Wu (CTO - Larkspur), Priya Menon (Head of AI), Aaron Lee (Infra)
Recording note: consent given

Auto-summary (auto-generated, optional):
- Larkspur is evaluating an exit/port from OpenAI/Azure toward a combination of hosted + dedicated Redwood capacity for cost predictability and compliance.
- Major concerns: SOC2/ISO, KMS/HSM, VPC/private deployment, eval parity with current vLLM/TGI stack, and 99th percentile latency during market hours.
- Agreed next steps include supplying security docs, scheduling technical benchmark, and providing prompt sets.

Topics: migration drivers, hosting options (hosted vs dedicated vs private), performance parity (vLLM/TGI), security/compliance, timelines

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you squeezing this in. i'm Samir with Redwood, account lead, and with me is maya our se. how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Daniel: good morning, thanks. i'm daniel, cto at larkspur. quick intro - priya runs the ai org, aaron is infra. we have about 10 people on the convo but we'll keep it tight.
[00:12] Priya: hey all, thanks. oriented to understanding how Redwood would match our current openai/azure setup and what the migration path looks like.
[00:18] Maya: great. quick agenda - we want to cover why you're exploring, your current stack and pain points, security/compliance needs, perf/latency expectations, and then suggest pilot steps. does that sound okay?
[00:26] Aaron: yes that's perfect. i'll probably ask the nitty infra questions.
[00:30] Samir: awesome. first, can you share the primary driver - cost, control, latency, or compliance?
[00:35] Daniel: couple things - cost at scale is big, yes. but also our compliance people are pushing for more control over data flows, and reliability during trading spikes. right now we use a mixture: some models on Azure OpenAI, some self-hosted vLLM for heavy workloads, and TGI experiments.
[00:46] Priya: and parity. the business won't accept regressions in answer quality - our NPS for assistant features is sensitive.
[00:52] Maya: totally, parity is a common ask. curious - when you say vllm for heavy workloads, are you running quantized INT8 or FP16 on your gpus?
[00:58] Priya: both. for most production endpoints we run int8 quantized Llama2 variants, sometimes fp16 for finetuned models. the vllm runtime gives us really low latency due to KV cache handy, but it's operationally heavy.
[01:10] Aaron: yep, our ops team spends time babysitting caching and memory fragmentation during bursts.
[01:15] Samir: that matches what we hear - folks trade ops complexity for latency. Redwood's offering is threefold: hosted api for fast onboarding, dedicated pools for predictable throughput, and private/vpc for locked-down networks. curious which of those resonates?
[01:28] Daniel: dedicated sounds interesting for predictable market-hour SLA, but we need VPC peering and key management.
[01:33] Aaron: encryption at rest and key control are musts - HSM or customer-managed KMS. also audit logs and retention controls.
[01:40] Maya: good callouts. we support KMS integrations and can run in a private deployment with customer-managed keys. audit logs and per-token tracing are part of console exports.
[01:48] Priya: on latency, we need 95th < 200ms and 99th < 350ms for 512 token context with our current quantized models. is that realistic on dedicated?
[01:59] Maya: for dedicated pools and with optimized kernels and batching tuned to your workload, yes we can hit those numbers; though it depends on batch size and concurrency. the parity tests we run measure quality delta and token throughput for sample prompts.
[02:11] Samir: also worth noting: when capacity is constrained we can route to a lower-cost model variant as fallback to preserve availability.
[02:18] Daniel: hmm fallback behavior is fine but we need deterministic failovers - auditably configured.
[02:23] Maya: we have rollout policies and can do canaries or strict A/B with rollout windows. config is stored and auditable.
[02:30] Aaron: about your hosted api - if we try hosted sandboxing, where does data land? do you retain prompts, and what's the retention default?
[02:39] Samir: by default hosted API does retain request/response logs for 30 days for debugging but we have options: we can disable retention for your account or set custom retention periods, and for enterprise private deployments data never touches Redwood's managed storage unless you opt in.
[02:54] Priya: ok good. we have legal saying no request logging for PII-sensitive flows.
[02:58] Maya: we can accommodate that - disable logging on routes or use private deployment. also we integrate with SSO/SAML and provide RBAC, so non-devs won't see logs.
[03:07] Daniel: what's the typical migration pattern? do teams lift-and-shift their prompts or retrain finetunes?
[03:13] Samir: most customers do a staged approach: 1) parity evals with same prompt sets on Redwood hosted sandbox; 2) run performance benchmarks on dedicated pools against vLLM/TGI using your quantized models; 3) gradually flip traffic using canary or route-based routing.
[03:27] Priya: about finetunes - we currently keep weights in-house and run finetunes on-prem. would we be able to serve customer-finetuned artifacts in private deployment?
[03:36] Maya: yes private deployment supports customer model artifacts and you can point to an internal model registry. we also support pinned model versions to avoid accidental updates.
[03:44] Aaron: network-wise - if we do private, we need IP allowlists and egress control. can you support VPC peering and static egress IP?
[03:52] Maya: yes, VPC peering is supported, and dedicated has static NAT addresses for egress. we also produce a network diagram and required ports for your infra team.
[04:01] Daniel: great. one friction we saw with Azure OpenAI was cold-start latency during autoscale - sometimes startup during a burst causes 500ms spikes. are your dedicated GPUs hot-warm managed to avoid cold starts?
[04:14] Maya: dedicated pools keep a warm pool by default based on SLA tier; we can reserve instance slots for your fleet during market hours. autoscaling is configurable for your burst windows.
[04:24] Priya: for eval parity - our ops track hallucination rate and an F1-like relevance metric on a benchmark corpus. acceptable delta is <3% relative to current. is that doable?
[04:35] Samir: yes we've had customers hit under 2% deltas when we tune quantization and kernel selection. part of the plan would be a parity run with your evaluation set and then an iterate pass.
[04:45] Aaron: on the topic of runtimes - you mentioned optimized kernels and kv cache. is that your own runtime or do you rely on vLLM/TGI under the hood?
[04:53] Maya: our serving runtime is a Redwood-optimized engine; we also support running models via TGI/vLLM in certain private setups for compatibility, but our hosted and dedicated runtimes include KV cache management and attention optimizations tuned per model. customers can bring vLLM artifacts too.
[05:07] Daniel: curious about tooling - how much observability do we get? we need token-level cost breakdowns and per-route latencies in the console for billing reconciliation.
[05:16] Maya: console shows token-level cost, per-model latency histograms, traces, and you can export per-route CSVs. we also have a tracing hook if you want to pull detailed spans into your existing observability.
[05:26] Priya: do you support structured function calling we rely on? our assistant uses function outputs to drive trades.
[05:32] Maya: yes function calls and structured outputs are supported, we also stream partial results for low-latency UX.
[05:38] Aaron: for proofs, can we run a 2-week pilot with a dedicated small pool and run the benchmarks? what's the cost model for that?
[05:44] Samir: we usually do a short pilot - hosted sandbox is free for initial parity tests, dedicated pilot has a time-limited reserved capacity fee that we discount for pilots. i'll propose numbers in the follow-up.
[05:53] Daniel: timeline wise we target a pilot in late november / early december and production cutover in q1 if things go well.
[05:59] Maya: makes sense. two technical clarifications from our side: please share sample prompt sets and any finetuned model formats (LLama, QLora, etc.) and also your current throughput during peak minutes.
[06:10] Priya: we'll share the prompts. our finetunes are QLoRA artifacts on Llama2-70B and some 13B for lower-cost paths.
[06:18] Aaron: peak qps is about 120 requests per second for user-facing assistant during market open bursts, with average 12 tokens per response.
[06:25] Samir: ok good data point. that concurrency suggests we tune batching carefully to minimize tail latency.
[06:30] [crosstalk] Daniel: also, curious about model size support - do you have memory-efficient hosting for >70B with int8?
[06:36] Maya: yes, int8 + partitioning + kv cache lets us host 70B-class, and for even larger we offer sharded serving.
[06:42] Priya: any customers who moved from vLLM/TGI to Redwood dedicated and saw parity? examples?
[06:48] Samir: a trading analytics customer moved last quarter; they ran parity suites and needed some kernel-level tuning to get token throughput right, but quality and tail latency matched within their 3% tolerance. happy to connect you to a reference, i'll check NDA constraints.
[07:02] Aaron: when you say kernel tuning, is that a hands-off thing from your ops or do we need to swap call patterns?
[07:08] Maya: we manage kernel selection and can collaborate with your team during the benchmark. often we adjust compile flags, sequence padding, and batching policy. it's collaborative but handled by our se team.
[07:18] Daniel: security - do you have SOC2 Type 2 and any financial services attestations?
[07:24] Samir: we have SOC2 Type 2 and are pursuing ISO attestation; for financial customers we offer private deployments and can do custom audits under an enterprise agreement.
[07:34] Priya: legal will want a data processing addendum and support for data residency in eu/us.
[07:40] Samir: yes DPA and contract options available. we can include residency controls on hosted accounts and of course private deployment stays within your VPC.
[07:47] Aaron: what's your incident response SLAs and runbooks? we need RTO/RPO for critical endpoints.
[07:53] Maya: we provide an SLA with uptime targets and have runbooks; for dedicated we can commit to specific SLOs and provide escalation contacts. i'll include a runbook excerpt in the security pack.
[08:02] Daniel: on billing, does token accounting match the same tokenization as OpenAI? we need deterministic billing for forecasting.
[08:09] Maya: we use BPE tokenization compatible with many open models but token counts can differ slightly. our console shows tokenized counts and cost per token; for contracts we can agree on a measurement method.
[08:19] Priya: one operational ask - can we bring our own telemetry exporter? we push spans to our jaeger/tempo stack.
[08:25] Maya: yes we have tracing hooks and can export spans or send to OTLP endpoints.
[08:30] Samir: ok want to talk briefly about the parity plan - maya, can you summarize the technical steps and metrics we'll run?
[08:36] Maya: sure. step 1: parity eval - run your benchmark corpus through current production and Redwood hosted sandbox; metrics: relevance F1, hallucination rate, latency p50/p95/p99. step 2: dedicated perf - spin up a small dedicated pool, deploy same quantized artifacts or run our quantization pipeline, measure throughput and tail latency under synthetic load that matches your 120 qps peak. step 3: iterate tuning - kernel flags, batching windows, and if needed we can suggest model variant (13b) for cost/latency tradeoff. expected duration 2 weeks for parity + tuning.
[09:05] Daniel: sounds reasonable. for the pilot, we need to ensure there are no data egress surprises - the legal team is sensitive.
[09:11] Samir: we can provide an egress and data flow diagram and sign a DPA that clarifies no-data-retention for routes you mark.
[09:18] Priya: one small thing - we use function calls that return structured json; ensure your streaming doesn't break partial json parsing in our handlers.
[09:25] Maya: streaming preserves function call boundaries; we'll validate with your integration tests.
[09:29] Aaron: on networking, do you support private link style connectivity for minimal exposure?
[09:34] Maya: yes private link / VPC peering options are available depending on region. will include specifics by region in follow-up.
[09:42] Daniel: any limitations we should know? e.g. certain ops disabled in private deployments?
[09:46] Maya: in fully air-gapped on-prem deployments some convenience features like hosted analytics may be limited, but we can ship a console connector or data export. most serving features are identical.
[09:56] Priya: for compliance we need to run a sample audit - can you provide log schema and retention controls?
[10:02] Samir: yes, will include log schema and sample audit logs with redaction.
[10:07] [silence 10s]
[10:17] Daniel: ok next steps - we'll collect prompts, share latency traces, and set up the technical deep dive with aaron and maya. legal will review your SOC2 pack.
[10:26] Samir: great. before we wrap any other questions?
[10:29] Priya: just one: can we get a cost model comparison - hosted token pricing vs dedicated committed cost?
[10:36] Samir: yes i'll send a high-level TCO calc showing token unit costs, reserved instance fees, and estimated monthly costs for your 120 qps pattern.
[10:44] Aaron: and include runway for burst capacity during big events.
[10:48] Samir: absolutely.
[10:50] Daniel: thanks everyone - this was useful.
[10:53] Samir: thanks all. we'll follow up with the pack and schedule.
[10:58] Maya: thanks - look forward to the deep dive.
[11:01] Priya: thanks.
[11:03] Aaron: bye.

Meeting close.
